questions.stem: Two quantities are said to be correlated when:

options.text: One is always exactly double the other
options.explanation: That is one particular exact relationship. Correlation covers any tendency to move together, not only a fixed multiple.

options.text: They tend to change together, so that a value of one gives information about the likely value of the other
options.explanation: Correct. Correlation is the tendency of two variables to move together; the coefficient measures the strength and direction of that tendency.

options.text: They are measured in the same units
options.explanation: The units are irrelevant. Height in cm and weight in kg can be strongly correlated though the units differ.

options.text: One is the cause of the other
options.explanation: Correlation implies neither cause nor effect. Two series can move together without one causing the other.

questions.stem: The price of a commodity and the quantity demanded of it usually show:

options.text: Positive correlation
options.explanation: Positive correlation would mean demand rises as price rises. Ordinary demand behaves the opposite way.

options.text: Zero correlation
options.explanation: There is a clear tendency, not none: higher prices go with lower demand.

options.text: Negative correlation
options.explanation: Correct. As price rises, quantity demanded tends to fall, so the two move in opposite directions — negative correlation.

options.text: Perfect positive correlation
options.explanation: The relationship is neither perfect nor positive; higher price is linked to lower, not higher, demand.

questions.stem: In a scatter diagram, all the plotted points lie exactly on a single straight line that slopes downward from left to right. The correlation coefficient is:

options.explanation: A value of +1 goes with an exact upward-sloping line, not a downward one.
Zero correlation shows as a shapeless cloud with no tilt, not an exact line.
Correct. Points exactly on a downward-sloping line show perfect negative correlation, r = −1.

options.text: Between 0 and +1
options.explanation: A downward line is negative, and an exact line is perfect, so the value is exactly −1, not a positive fraction.

questions.sourceRef: Scatter diagram and the sign and size of r

questions.stem: Which of the following can NEVER be a value of the Karl Pearson coefficient of correlation?

options.explanation: This lies inside −1 to +1 and is a perfectly valid strong negative correlation.
Zero is valid; it means no linear correlation.
This is a valid strong positive correlation.
Correct. The correlation coefficient always satisfies −1 ≤ r ≤ 1, so 1.20 is impossible and signals an arithmetic error.

questions.stem: The coefficient of correlation is:

options.text: Independent of change of origin but not of change of scale
options.explanation: It is independent of both. A change of scale by a positive factor leaves r unchanged.

options.text: Independent of both change of origin and change of scale (a negative scale factor only reverses its sign)
options.explanation: Correct. Shifting the origin never changes r, and rescaling by a positive factor never changes it; a negative scale factor keeps the size but flips the sign.

options.text: Dependent on both change of origin and change of scale
options.explanation: Neither move changes r. This is exactly why the assumed-mean short form is valid.

options.text: Independent of change of scale but not of change of origin
options.explanation: The reverse of the truth. A change of origin has no effect at all on r.

questions.sourceRef: r is independent of change of origin and scale

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Karl Pearson r · From data
questions.stem: For the pairs x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 3, 2, 5, 6, 4, the Karl Pearson coefficient of correlation is:

options.explanation: Perfect correlation would need all points on one line; here the scatter is only moderate.
This is r², the product of the two regression coefficients, not r itself. Take the square root.
Correct. Numerator nΣxy − (Σx)(Σy) = 5×66 − 15×20 = 30; each bracket is 50, so r = 30 ÷ √(50×50) = 0.6.
This divides the numerator 30 by 100 (using (Σx)² and (Σy)² directly) instead of by √(50×50). The denominator is the root of the product of the two brackets.

questions.stem: For the pairs x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 3, 2, 5, 6, 4, the covariance of x and y, Cov(x, y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ n, is:

options.explanation: This is Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) before dividing by n. Divide the total of 6 by n = 5.
Correct. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 6, and dividing by n = 5 gives Cov(x, y) = 1.2.
0.6 is the correlation coefficient here, not the covariance. Covariance still carries the units of x times y.
30 is nΣxy − (Σx)(Σy). Covariance is that divided by n², or equivalently the mean of the deviation products, giving 1.2.

questions.sourceRef: Cov(x, y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ n

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Karl Pearson r · From sums
questions.stem: For 5 pairs of values the sums are Σx = 30, Σy = 38, Σxy = 264, Σx² = 220 and Σy² = 330. The coefficient of correlation is nearest to:

options.explanation: Perfect correlation is not reached; the points do not lie exactly on a line.
0.90 is the regression coefficient b_yx = 180 ÷ 200. The correlation coefficient divides by the root of the product of both brackets, giving 0.8868.
This uses the wrong denominator. r = 180 ÷ √(200×206) = 0.8868, not 0.79.

questions.sourceRef: r from the five raw sums

questions.stem: For 5 pairs the sums are Σx = 30, Σy = 38, Σxy = 264, Σx² = 220 and Σy² = 330. The regression coefficient of y on x, b_yx, is:

options.explanation: 0.87 is b_xy = 180 ÷ 206, which divides by the y term. b_yx divides by the x term, nΣx² − (Σx)² = 200.
0.6 is not this data's coefficient. Here b_yx = 180 ÷ 200 = 0.9.
This inverts the ratio, dividing 200 by 180. The numerator is the common numerator 180, the denominator is the x term 200.
Correct. b_yx = [nΣxy − (Σx)(Σy)] ÷ [nΣx² − (Σx)²] = 180 ÷ 200 = 0.9.

questions.stem: For the pairs x = 6, 2, 10, 4, 8 and y = 9, 11, 5, 8, 7, the regression coefficient of x on y, b_xy, is:

options.explanation: −0.92 is the correlation coefficient r for this data, not the regression coefficient of x on y.
−0.65 is b_yx, which divides by the x term (200). b_xy divides by the y term (100), giving −1.3.
The sign is wrong. The numerator −130 is negative, so b_xy is negative: the two variables move in opposite directions.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Link r and b · Geometric mean
questions.stem: The two regression coefficients are b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 0.45. The coefficient of correlation is:

options.explanation: This is the arithmetic mean of the two coefficients, not r. The correlation is the geometric mean, √(0.8 × 0.45).
0.36 is r², the product b_yx × b_xy. Take its square root to get r.
Correct. r = +√(b_yx × b_xy) = √(0.8 × 0.45) = √0.36 = 0.6, positive because both coefficients are positive.
This adds the coefficients. A correlation cannot exceed 1 in any case; r is the geometric mean, 0.6.

readLink.label: Read: Linking r and the coefficients, §9 →

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Link r and b · Sign
questions.stem: Both regression coefficients are negative: b_yx = −0.6 and b_xy = −0.6. The coefficient of correlation is:

options.explanation: The size is right but the sign is wrong. When both regression coefficients are negative, r takes the negative root.
Correct. r = ±√(b_yx × b_xy) = √0.36 = 0.6 in size, and the common sign of the two coefficients is negative, so r = −0.6.
−0.36 is the product with a sign attached, not r. r is the square root of the product, with the coefficients' sign.
Two non-zero coefficients cannot give zero correlation. Here r = −0.6.

questions.sourceRef: Sign of r is the common sign of the two regression coefficients

questions.stem: Which statement about the two regression coefficients is always TRUE?

options.text: They always have the same sign, which is the sign of r
options.explanation: Correct. The two coefficients share the common numerator, so they carry the same sign, and that sign is the sign of r.

options.text: One is always positive and the other always negative
options.explanation: They can never have opposite signs, because they share a numerator.

options.text: Both always lie between −1 and +1
options.explanation: A regression coefficient may exceed 1 in size; only r is bounded by ±1.

options.text: They are always equal to each other
options.explanation: They are equal only when the two spreads are equal. In general b_yx ≠ b_xy.

questions.sourceRef: Both regression coefficients carry the sign of r

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Regression coefficient · From r and SDs
questions.stem: Given r = 0.8, standard deviation of x = 4 and standard deviation of y = 6, the regression coefficient of y on x, b_yx, is:

options.explanation: 0.53 is b_xy = r × σx ÷ σy = 0.8 × 4 ÷ 6. For b_yx the ratio is σy ÷ σx.
This multiplies r by σy alone (0.8 × 6). The formula divides σy by σx as well.
0.8 is r itself. The regression coefficient scales r by the ratio of the standard deviations.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Regression coefficient · From r and SDs
questions.stem: Given r = 0.7, standard deviation of x = 5 and standard deviation of y = 10, the regression coefficient of x on y, b_xy, is:

options.explanation: 1.4 is b_yx = r × σy ÷ σx = 0.7 × 10 ÷ 5. For b_xy the ratio is σx ÷ σy.
0.7 is r itself, before scaling by the ratio of the standard deviations.
This multiplies r by σx alone (0.7 × 5). Divide by σy as well to get 0.35.

questions.stem: The regression line of y on x is y = 0.6x + 2.2. The estimated value of y when x = 10 is:

options.explanation: This uses only 0.6 × 10 and drops the intercept 2.2. Add the constant term of the line.
This adds 0.6 and 2.2 and treats x as 1. Substitute x = 10 into the line.
This mishandles the slope. With slope 0.6 and intercept 2.2, x = 10 gives 8.2.

This is the given y, not the estimate of x. Substitute y = 9 into the line.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Regression lines · Point of means
questions.stem: The two regression lines are 3x + 2y = 26 and 6x + y = 31. The mean value of x is:

options.explanation: This does not satisfy both equations. The consistent solution is x = 4, y = 7.
7 is the mean of y, not of x. Solving the two equations gives x̄ = 4 and ȳ = 7.
Correct. The lines meet at the means. Solving 3x + 2y = 26 and 6x + y = 31 gives x̄ = 4 (and ȳ = 7).
13 does not solve the pair. Substitute back to check: x = 4 gives 6×4 + y = 31, so y = 7.

questions.sourceRef: Both regression lines pass through (x̄, ȳ)

questions.stem: The two regression lines for a set of paired data always:

options.text: Are parallel to each other
options.explanation: They are parallel only in the impossible case of never meeting; in fact they always intersect at the means.

options.text: Intersect at the point of means (x̄, ȳ)
options.explanation: Correct. Whatever the data, both lines pass through the mean of x and the mean of y, so they cross there.

options.text: Pass through the origin (0, 0)
options.explanation: They pass through the origin only by coincidence. In general they pass through (x̄, ȳ).

options.text: Have the same slope
options.explanation: Equal slopes would make them the same line, which happens only when r = ±1.

questions.sourceRef: The two lines cross at (x̄, ȳ)

questions.stem: Six items are ranked by two judges. The rank differences are d = −1, 1, −1, 1, −1, 1. The rank correlation coefficient is nearest to:

options.explanation: This does not follow from Σd² = 6 and n = 6. The correct value is 1 − 36 ÷ 210 = 0.8286.
0.17 is 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)], the quantity subtracted from 1. R itself is 1 minus that.
The sign is wrong. Small rank differences give a high positive R, not a negative one.

questions.stem: Seven paintings are ranked by two judges. The rank differences are d = −2, 1, −1, 2, −1, 1, 0. The rank correlation coefficient is nearest to:

options.explanation: 0.21 is the fraction subtracted from 1 (72 ÷ 336). R is 1 minus that, 0.7857.
0.86 would follow from Σd² = 8. Here Σd² = 12, giving R = 0.7857.
This uses the wrong denominator. With n = 7, the denominator is 7 × 48 = 336, not a smaller figure.

questions.stem: Two examiners mark five candidates. Examiner X awards 50, 70, 60, 60, 80 and Examiner Y awards 55, 60, 40, 55, 60. Using average ranks and the tie correction, the rank correlation coefficient is:

options.explanation: 0.75 omits the tie correction (using Σd² = 5 alone). The corrected Σd² is 6.5, giving 0.675.
This does not match the corrected calculation. With corrected Σd² = 6.5 and n = 5, R = 0.675.
0.325 is the fraction subtracted from 1 (39 ÷ 120), not R itself.
Correct. Σd² = 5; tie correction = 0.5 (X) + 1.0 (Y) = 1.5; corrected Σd² = 6.5; R = 1 − (6×6.5) ÷ 120 = 0.675.

questions.sourceRef: Rank correlation with tie correction Σ(m³ − m) ÷ 12

questions.stem: A correlation coefficient of 0.6 is obtained from 64 pairs of observations. The probable error is nearest to:

options.explanation: This forgets to square r, using (1 − r) = 0.4 instead of (1 − r²) = 0.64. The formula squares r.
This omits the division by √n. Divide 0.6745 × 0.64 by 8.
0.34 is 6 × PE, the significance threshold, not the probable error itself.

questions.stem: Under the probable-error rule of thumb, a sample correlation r is treated as significant when:

options.text: r is less than the probable error
options.explanation: That is the test for NOT significant — r could easily be zero.

options.text: r equals the probable error
options.explanation: Equality gives no firm verdict; it is well below the significance threshold.

options.text: r is greater than six times the probable error
options.explanation: Correct. The rule of thumb treats correlation as significant when r exceeds 6 × PE, and as not significant when r is below PE.

options.text: the probable error is greater than 1
options.explanation: The probable error is a small positive number here; it is not compared with 1. Compare r with PE and with 6 × PE.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes correlation from regression?

options.text: Correlation measures the strength of the relationship; regression provides an equation to estimate one variable from the other
options.explanation: Correct. Correlation gives one number for strength and direction; regression gives lines that let you estimate one variable from another.

options.text: Correlation gives two lines; regression gives one number
options.explanation: The reverse. Correlation gives one number, r; regression gives two lines.

options.text: Both give exactly the same information
options.explanation: They share the same sums but answer different questions — strength versus estimation.

options.text: Correlation depends on units; regression does not
options.explanation: It is the other way round. r is a pure number; regression coefficients carry units.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Regression coefficients · Finding an SD
questions.stem: Given b_yx = 1.6, b_xy = 0.4 and the standard deviation of x = 3, the standard deviation of y is:

options.explanation: This multiplies σx by b_yx ÷ b_xy = 4. The ratio of the standard deviations is √4 = 2, so σy = 6.
This takes σx ÷ σy the wrong way. Since σy² ÷ σx² = 4, σy is twice σx, giving 6.
Correct. b_yx ÷ b_xy = σy² ÷ σx² = 1.6 ÷ 0.4 = 4, so σy ÷ σx = 2 and σy = 2 × 3 = 6.
This multiplies σx by b_yx (1.6). The correct route uses b_yx ÷ b_xy = σy² ÷ σx².

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Karl Pearson r · From covariance
questions.stem: The covariance of x and y is 12, the standard deviation of x is 4 and the standard deviation of y is 5. The coefficient of correlation is:

options.explanation: This divides by σx² and σy in some mix. The denominator is σx × σy = 20, giving 0.6.
This divides 12 by σy alone (5) and mishandles it. Divide by the product σx × σy = 20.
0.75 is Cov ÷ σx² = 12 ÷ 16, the regression coefficient b_yx, not r.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Regression coefficient · From covariance and variance
questions.stem: The covariance of x and y is 12 and the variance of x is 16. The regression coefficient of y on x, b_yx, is:

options.explanation: Correct. b_yx = Cov(x, y) ÷ σx² = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75.
This inverts the ratio, dividing 16 by 12. b_yx divides the covariance by the variance of x.
0.6 would need a standard deviation of y as well. b_yx uses only Cov and the variance of x, giving 0.75.
This multiplies covariance by variance. The regression coefficient divides Cov by σx².

questions.stem: The two regression lines coincide (become a single line) when:

options.explanation: When r = 0 the two lines are perpendicular, not coincident.
Correct. Perfect correlation makes both lines the same line; the two coefficients become reciprocals and the slopes match.

options.text: the means are equal
options.explanation: Equal means fix where the lines cross, not whether they coincide. Coincidence needs r = ±1.

options.text: the two standard deviations are equal
options.explanation: Equal standard deviations make the two coefficients equal, but the lines still differ unless r = ±1.

questions.stem: When the coefficient of correlation is zero, the two regression lines are:

options.text: The same line
options.explanation: They become one line only when r = ±1, not when r = 0.

options.text: Parallel
options.explanation: They still cross at the means, so they are not parallel.

options.text: At right angles to each other
options.explanation: Correct. When r = 0 the two lines are perpendicular — one horizontal, one vertical — reflecting no linear relationship.

options.text: Both passing through the origin
options.explanation: They pass through the means, and only through the origin by coincidence. At r = 0 they are perpendicular.

questions.stem: The two regression lines are 8x − 10y + 66 = 0 and 40x − 18y − 214 = 0. The mean value of y is:

options.explanation: 13 is the mean of x, not of y. Solving the two equations gives x̄ = 13 and ȳ = 17.
Correct. The lines meet at the means. Solving 8x − 10y = −66 and 40x − 18y = 214 gives ȳ = 17 (and x̄ = 13).
7 does not satisfy both equations. Substitute to check: x = 13, y = 17 solves both.
6.6 is the intercept of one line written in slope form, not a mean. The mean of y is 17.

questions.stem: There are two regression lines for a pair of variables because:

options.text: One estimates y from x by minimising vertical errors, and the other estimates x from y by minimising horizontal errors
options.explanation: Correct. The line of y on x minimises squared errors in y; the line of x on y minimises squared errors in x. They minimise different errors, so they are different lines.

options.text: One is for positive correlation and the other for negative correlation
options.explanation: Both lines exist for any data, whatever the sign of the correlation.

options.text: One uses the mean and the other uses the median
options.explanation: Both least-squares lines pass through the mean point; neither uses the median.

options.text: The data are always split into two halves
options.explanation: The data are not split. Both lines use all the pairs; they simply minimise error in different variables.

questions.topic: Ch 17 · Link r and b · Geometric mean
questions.stem: The two regression coefficients are b_yx = 0.2 and b_xy = 1.8. The coefficient of correlation is:

options.explanation: 0.36 is the product b_yx × b_xy, which equals r². Take its square root to get r.
Correct. r = +√(0.2 × 1.8) = √0.36 = 0.6, positive because both coefficients are positive.
This is the arithmetic mean of the two coefficients, not r. The correlation is the geometric mean, 0.6.
This adds the coefficients. r = √(0.2 × 1.8) = 0.6.

questions.stem: A correlation coefficient of 0.9 is obtained from 100 pairs of observations. The probable error is nearest to:

options.explanation: 0.077 is about 6 × PE, the significance threshold, not the probable error itself.
This uses (1 − r) = 0.1 instead of (1 − r²) = 0.19. The formula squares r.
This omits the division by √n. Divide 0.6745 × 0.19 by 10.

questions.stem: If one regression coefficient is greater than 1, then the other regression coefficient must be:

options.text: Also greater than 1
options.explanation: That would make the product exceed 1, but the product equals r² and cannot exceed 1. So the other must be smaller.

options.text: Less than 1
options.explanation: Correct. Since b_yx × b_xy = r² ≤ 1, if one coefficient exceeds 1 the other must be less than 1 to keep the product at most 1.

options.text: Equal to 1
options.explanation: It need not equal 1; it need only be small enough that the product stays at most 1.

options.text: Negative
options.explanation: The two coefficients share a sign. If one is positive and above 1, the other is positive and below 1, not negative.

questions.stem: To estimate the value of y for a given value of x, you should use:

options.text: The average of the two lines
options.explanation: There is no averaging step. Use the line of y on x to estimate y.

options.text: The regression line of x on y
options.explanation: That line estimates x from y, the opposite task. Using it here gives a different, wrong estimate unless r = ±1.

options.text: Either line, since both give the same answer
options.explanation: The two lines have different slopes and give different answers, except when r = ±1.

options.text: The regression line of y on x
options.explanation: Correct. The line of y on x is fitted to estimate y from x, so it is the right line for this prediction.
